papers.title: Complete reference genomes track disease notoriety, not burden: a burden–genome mismatch for priority zoonoses along China's land border
papers.abstract: Abstract Complete reference genomes are essential for molecular diagnosis, typing, and source-tracing; yet their availability for the zoonoses that cause the greatest disease burden is seldom assessed. Along China's land border, where a heterogeneous set of priority zoonoses circulates, we investigated whether complete reference-genome resources correspond to disease burden. For 15 border-priority zoonoses, we compiled disease burden (using notifiable-disease cases from China CDC and animal events from WAHIS), complete-genome availability (from NCBI), and research output (from PubMed) as a secondary metric. We evaluated the relationship between burden and genome availability and verified its robustness using different genome metrics, a leave-one-out jackknife procedure, an exact permutation test, and alternative burden definitions, while also revealing a genome-metric paradox. Among the six diseases with official Chinese human-incidence data, complete reference genomes exhibited a strong inverse correlation with burden (Spearman ρ = −0.94; exact permutation p = 0.001): brucellosis, the highest-burden zoonosis (67 418 cases in 2024), had only 4 complete genomes, whereas low-burden rabies (170 cases) had 2 740. This relationship remained stable when excluding any single disease (ρ = −0.90 to −1.0), incorporating animal burden (ρ = −0.89), or employing a viral-record metric. Importantly, the association depended on the use of complete genomes: total assembly counts (which include numerous draft genomes) yielded an opposite correlation ρ = +0.71. Thus, the finding pertains specifically to finished-quality reference genomes rather than total sequencing efforts, and we explicitly report this paradox. The high-burden, genome-poor group included both bacterial and viral pathogens, precluding a taxonomic artefact. Research output (uncapped PubMed totals) showed no significant relationship with burden (ρ = −0.26, p = 0.6). Nine of the 15 border zoonoses lacked any official Chinese human-incidence data. Conclusions: Along China's border, complete reference genomes for priority zoonoses reflect pathogen notoriety rather than disease burden. Investment in finished reference genomes for high-burden, genome-poor zoonoses such as brucellosis would enhance their molecular diagnosis, typing, and source-tracing capabilities.

For 15 border-priority zoonoses, we compiled disease burden (using notifiable-disease cases from China CDC and animal events from WAHIS), complete-genome availability (from NCBI), and research output (from PubMed) as a secondary metric. We evaluated the relationship between burden and genome availability and verified its robustness using different genome metrics, a leave-one-out jackknife procedure, an exact permutation test, and alternative burden definitions, while also revealing a genome-metric paradox. Among the six diseases with official Chinese human-incidence data, complete reference genomes exhibited a strong inverse correlation with burden (Spearman ρ = −0.94; exact permutation p = 0.001): brucellosis, the highest-burden zoonosis (67 418 cases in 2024), had only 4 complete genomes, whereas low-burden rabies (170 cases) had 2 740. This relationship remained stable when excluding any single disease (ρ = −0.90 to −1.0), incorporating animal burden (ρ = −0.89), or employing a viral-record metric. Importantly, the association depended on the use of complete genomes: total assembly counts (which include numerous draft genomes) yielded an opposite correlation ρ = +0.71. Thus, the finding pertains specifically to finished-quality reference genomes rather than total sequencing efforts, and we explicitly report this paradox. The high-burden, genome-poor group included both bacterial and viral pathogens, precluding a taxonomic artefact. Research output (uncapped PubMed totals) showed no significant relationship with burden (ρ = −0.26, p = 0.6). Nine of the 15 border zoonoses lacked any official Chinese human-incidence data. Conclusions: Along China's border, complete reference genomes for priority zoonoses reflect pathogen notoriety rather than disease burden. Investment in finished reference genomes for high-burden, genome-poor zoonoses such as brucellosis would enhance their molecular diagnosis, typing, and source-tracing capabilities.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the gap in understanding whether complete reference genomes for zoonoses align with their disease burden, as molecular diagnosis and source-tracing rely on such resources but their availability is rarely evaluated against burden metrics.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study focused on 15 priority zoonoses along China's land border, examining the relationship between their disease burden and the availability of complete reference genomes. It included both bacterial and viral pathogens, ensuring a diverse representation of potential zoonotic diseases.
analysis.methods: Researchers compiled data on disease burden from Chinese notifiable-disease cases and animal events, complete-genome availability from NCBI, and research output from PubMed. They evaluated the relationship between burden and genome availability using statistical methods, including a leave-one-out jackknife procedure, exact permutation test, and alternative burden definitions.
analysis.main_results: Among the six diseases with official Chinese human-incidence data, complete reference genomes showed a strong inverse correlation with burden (Spearman ρ = −0.94; exact permutation p = 0.001). Brucellosis, the highest-burden zoonosis, had only 4 complete genomes, while rabies, a low-burden disease, had 2,740.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that complete reference genomes for priority zoonoses reflect notoriety rather than burden, highlighting a paradox where high-burden diseases have fewer complete genomes, and the relationship remains stable even when excluding individual diseases or incorporating animal burden.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that investment in complete reference genomes for high-burden, genome-poor zoonoses like brucellosis could improve molecular diagnosis, typing, and source-tracing, which are critical for effective public health responses.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study's evidence is based on abstract-only data, and the relationship between burden and genome availability was assessed using statistical methods. The association was found to depend on the use of complete genomes, not total sequencing efforts, which limits generalizability to other contexts.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates whether complete reference genomes for zoonoses along China's land border correspond to their disease burden. It finds a strong inverse correlation between burden and genome availability, with high-burden diseases like brucellosis having fewer complete genomes compared to low-burden diseases like rabies. The relationship remains stable even when excluding individual diseases or incorporating animal burden. The authors emphasize that the findings pertain specifically to finished-quality reference genomes, not total sequencing efforts, and highlight the importance of investing in genome resources for high-burden, genome-poor zoonoses to enhance molecular diagnosis and source-tracing capabilities. The study's evidence is based on abstract-only data, and the results are supported by statistical analyses, though the findings may not be generalizable beyond the specific context of China's border zoonoses.

elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,针对布鲁氏菌病等高负担、基因组 缺乏的人畜共患病,投资完整的参考 基因组 可以改善分子 基因组、分型和来源追踪,这对于有效的公共卫生应对措施至关重要。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的证据基于仅摘要数据,并使用统计方法评估了负担与 基因组 可用性之间的关系。研究发现这种关联依赖于完整 基因组 的使用,而不是总测序工作,这限制了对其他上下文的普遍适用性。

papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 完整的参考文献 基因组 对于分子 诊断、打字和来源追踪至关重要;然而,人们很少评估它们对造成最大疾病负担的人畜共患疾病的可用性。沿着中国陆地边界,多种优先人畜共患病在该地区传播,我们调查了完整的参考 基因组 资源是否与疾病负担相对应。对于 15 种边境优先人畜共患病,我们编制了疾病负担(使用中国 CDC 的法定疾病病例和 WAHIS 的动物事件)、完整的 基因组 可用性(来自 NCBI)和研究成果(来自 PubMed)作为次要指标。我们评估了负担和 基因组 可用性之间的关系,并使用不同的 基因组 指标、留一折刀程序、精确排列测试和替代负担定义验证了其稳健性,同时还揭示了 基因组 指标悖论。在具有中国官方人类发病率数据的六种疾病中,完整参考基因组与负担呈现强烈的负相关(Spearman ρ = -0.94;精确排列p = 0.001):负担最高的人兽共患病(2024年为67 418例)布鲁氏菌病只有4个完整的基因组,而低负担 狂犬病(170 例)有 2 740 例。当排除任何单一疾病(ρ = -0.90 至 -1.0)、纳入动物负担(ρ = -0.89)或采用病毒记录指标时,这种关系保持稳定。重要的是,该关联取决于完整 基因组 的使用:总装配计数(包括大量 基因组 草稿)产生相反的相关性 ρ = +0.71。因此,这一发现具体涉及成品质量参考 基因组,而不是总体测序工作,我们明确报告了这一悖论。高负担、基因组 贫困组包括细菌和病毒病原体,排除了分类学假象。研究成果(不设上限的 PubMed 总数)与负担没有显着关系(ρ = -0.26,p = 0.6)。15 种边境人畜共患病中有 9 种缺乏中国官方人类 发病率 数据。结论:在中国边境,重点人畜共患病的完整参考 基因组 反映了病原体的恶名而不是疾病负担。对高负担、基因组 缺乏的人畜共患病(如布鲁氏菌病)的成品参考 基因组 的投资将增强其分子 基因组、分型和来源追踪能力。

papers.abstract: According to Santos and Tellería (2006), these types of processes have numerous consequences: regional habitat loss and the resulting reduction in the size of affected organism populations, decreasing the regional density of species; an increase in the distance between fragments, hindering the exchange of individuals between isolated populations for the purpose of replenishment; and greater exposure of the fragmented habitat to multiple interferences from surrounding habitats (habitat matrix), resulting in a growing "edge effect" that causes a decline in habitat quality, affecting the survival of populations residing in the fragments. The reduction, fragmentation, and deterioration of habitat ultimately lead to the atomization of original distributions into increasingly smaller and more isolated subpopulations, resulting, in situations where the problem progresses unabated, in landscapes where many of the original species are missing (Santos and Tellería, 2006).Considering the "One Health" approach, it is important to understand that this environmental impact and its consequences for animal habitats also create problems for the surrounding communities or even those that live alongside them. This is because human-animal relationships become more complex with each generation. Although animals continue to fulfill a utilitarian role in human life (the food industry, animal breeding and sales, among others), they are affected by the environmental controls implemented by humanity due to their susceptibility (Gutiérrez et al., 2007). This leads to a normalization, evolution, and narrowing of human-animal interaction with species that should not be in this situation. These species are influenced by territorial transformations, human convenience, and also by the affectionate relationships that develop with them due to the insensitivity caused by convenience, ignorance, or ideology (Gutiérrez et al., 2007;Santos and Tellería, 2006). However, this also has negative consequences for human beings. (2022) state, these situations carry risks for the community, such as zoonoses, consequences that arise from compromising or threatening the environment. This creates conditions that foster a breeding ground for disease by making it unhealthy for life, since human health is not independent of the health of other organisms. This is where the importance of a comprehensive approach that considers all the components of One Health comes in (Lampert et al., 2022).Understanding the importance of the integrity of all actors within a community allows for a different perspective on the relevance of territorial transformations and urban planning to health risks. The approach of canids to urban areas is directly related to anthropogenic processes. Temporal interactions and competition between species even arise depending on variables such as housing density and forest cover (Pearson et al., 2022). The consequences of urbanization, which accompany changes in land use, the incorporation of substances to enhance soil productivity, and habitat loss and fragmentation, modify the distribution of carnivorous mammals (Pereira et al., 2024). Furthermore, the potential consumption of these animals by humans is another factor that can influence the presence of wild mammals in areas currently inhabited by humans (Pereira et al., 2024;Lampert, 2025). All these factors contribute to the loss of biodiversity, which is accompanied by the loss of natural habitats, the reorganization of communities (Pereira et al., 2025), and the nutritional and metabolic problems associated with the intake of ultra-processed foods that are typical of human beings (Lampert, 2025).Human activities that influence the interaction of canids are affected by their sensitivity. This sensitivity to humans was demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. One study showed that gray foxes (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), and coyotes (Canis latrans) modified their daily activities in both urban and rural areas (Allen et al., 2025). Gray foxes were the canids that exhibited the greatest change in daily activity during the pandemic (Allen et al., 2025).For example, the Pampas gray fox (Lycalopex gymnocercus) is one of the most widespread and abundant wild canids in Argentina. This animal is a clear example of the importance of One Health education, based on the One Health approach. Temporal interactions and competition between species even arise depending on variables such as housing density and forest cover (Pearson et al., 2022). The consequences of urbanization, which accompany changes in land use, the incorporation of substances to enhance soil productivity, and habitat loss and fragmentation, modify the distribution of carnivorous mammals (Pereira et al., 2024). Furthermore, the potential consumption of these animals by humans is another factor that can influence the presence of wild mammals in areas currently inhabited by humans (Pereira et al., 2024;Lampert, 2025). All these factors contribute to the loss of biodiversity, which is accompanied by the loss of natural habitats, the reorganization of communities (Pereira et al., 2025), and the nutritional and metabolic problems associated with the intake of ultra-processed foods that are typical of human beings (Lampert, 2025).Human activities that influence the interaction of canids are affected by their sensitivity. This sensitivity to humans was demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic. One study showed that gray foxes (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), red foxes (Vulpes vulpes), and coyotes (Canis latrans) modified their daily activities in both urban and rural areas (Allen et al., 2025). Gray foxes modified their daily activities in rural areas, while coyotes modified theirs in urban areas (Allen et al., 2025). Gray foxes were the canids that exhibited the greatest change in daily activity during the pandemic (Allen et al., 2025).For example, the Pampas gray fox (Lycalopex gymnocercus) is one of the most widespread and abundant wild canids in Argentina. However, it is common to see news reports of this species being found in urban areas. This can pose a potential risk for the transmission of parasitic zoonotic diseases. A study conducted in the Province of Buenos Aires found that of 142 foxes found dead and/or captured, the digestive tract harbored 16 species of helminths (4 cestodes, 1 trematode, and 11 nematodes) and 9 species of protozoa (Scioscia, 2022). Furthermore, the Pampas gray fox is a host for E. bohemi (Scioscia et al., 2018). Furthermore, another study mentions the presence of Neospora caninum in the animal. This is of great concern given that it is a protozoan that causes abortions and reproductive failures in livestock, resulting in significant economic losses (Scioscia et al., 2022). In Argentina, there are various reports of the appearance of the pampas gray fox in urban and rural areas inhabited by people. Urban expansion into natural habitats is leading to increasingly close contact between humans and native wildlife, which can result in the transmission of zoonotic diseases. Given this situation, education plays a crucial role in prevention.The Pampas gray fox is of great ecological importance. Its role as a predator, scavenger, frugivore, and seed disperser has contributed to the development of diverse biomes (Vidal et al., 2025). This animal is a clear example of the importance of One Health education, based on the One Health approach. From an educational perspective, the Science, Technology, and Society (STS) approach is a valuable tool for fostering critical thinking in students, contextualizing learning, and enabling the community to understand different perspectives on an animal. Lampert (2025) has written a book titled "When the Jungle Sits Down to Eat," which analyzes how the welfare of coatis (Nasua nasua), the prevalence of zoonoses, and their behavior are affected by human interaction in Iguazu National Park (Misiones Province, Argentina). Previous research has demonstrated that classroom-based approaches to animal ecology, behavior, welfare, and health risks foster the development of critical thinking skills to prevent contact (Lampert, 2025). While this research focused on the coati, it is essential to address this educational topic with each species that arrives in urban areas, focusing on prevention. Furthermore, various interviews and studies have shown that people become more aware of the potential negative effects of interaction on the animal, rather than on themselves. Therefore, One Health education for prevention must focus not only on people, but also on the risk to species.For the Pampas gray fox, the issue of domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) is a factor within the broader context of habitat alteration. Furthermore, the Pampas gray fox frequently ventures into these areas due to their proximity to its natural habitat. Consequently, the level of risk differs between urban and rural zones, although the recent expansion of gated communities has narrowed this gap. It is also worth noting that many canids in rural areas often feed on animal offal; this practice can increase the risk of pathogen transmission to other species-such as the Pampas gray fox-and even directly to humans. Therefore, the aim is to improve understanding of the spatiotemporal patterns of interspecific contact between invasive and native carnivores, in order to prevent the spread of various pathogens (Hernández et al., 2021). It is worth noting that this education must be contextualized within the specific settings where pathogen transmission is likely to occur. Hence the importance of raising awareness about zoonoses in the various spaces shared by humans and animals, as well as among different animal species. The interaction between animals, humans, and their habitats should be a central focus of modern scientific education; the goal is not merely to learn the definitions and characteristics of various zoonoses, but to understand the environments in which transmission takes place. This enables the public to become informed-for instance, on how to act when encountering animals.In the case of the Pampas Gray Fox, human intervention is impacting its ecology through the use of poison, hunting, roads, and urbanization. This leads us to consider this animal as a model for understanding the capacity to govern shared life with integrity, maintaining ecological and health functions in balance (Vidal et al., 2025). Therefore, education must promote conservation by raising awareness of the human-caused problems affecting this animal and their potential solutions, such as banning poisons, reducing roadkill, managing domestic animals, and promoting coexistence under a genuine "One Health, One Wellbeing" approach, as described by Vidal et al. (2025), in order to achieve the integration of human, animal, and environmental health in urban planning.The STS approach to one health prevention education should incorporate the following elements, drawing on the book of Lampert (2019): Mainstream the "One Health, One Wellbeing" or Conservation Medicine approach. In the case of the Pampas gray fox, education regarding the animal should not be conducted in isolation-treating the animal's physiology and habitat, zoonoses, and territorial/urban expansion as separate topics. Instead, the issue must be addressed through an integrated, cross-cutting approach that acknowledges its complexity.  Contextualize instruction across different settings. Studying and understanding human-animal contact differs depending on whether the setting is rural, peri-urban, or urban. Local wildlife must be identified, along with the ways in which the transmission of microorganisms between species could be altered.  Teach about animal feeding practices. It is essential to understand the risks posed to the ecosystem by feeding domestic canids animal offal or raw meat that has not undergone sanitary or food safety inspection.  Develop educational initiatives grounded in health education, environmental education, and food education. In the case of Argentina, it is worth noting that environmental education and food education are mandated by law.

papers.title_original: Territorial expansion and parasitic zoonoses: the pampas gray fox in Argentina as a case study and its educational potential for prevention

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the impact of territorial expansion on parasitic zoonoses, particularly focusing on the Pampas gray fox in Argentina and its implications for human and animal health.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examined the effects of urban expansion and habitat fragmentation on the Pampas gray fox population in Argentina, analyzing interactions between the species and human communities.
analysis.methods: The study referenced previous research on the behavioral and ecological changes of canids in response to human activities and included data from studies on the presence of parasitic zoonoses in the Pampas gray fox.
analysis.main_results: During the COVID-19 pandemic, gray foxes modified their daily activities, and the Pampas gray fox was found to host various helminths and protozoa, including Neospora caninum, which causes abortions and reproductive failures in livestock.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings highlight the ecological and health risks associated with the territorial expansion and human-animal interactions, emphasizing the need for a One Health approach to address these issues.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The study underscores the importance of understanding the ecological role of the Pampas gray fox and its potential to transmit zoonotic diseases, informing public health strategies and educational initiatives.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on general observations and references to prior studies, which may limit the confidence in specific causal relationships or direct findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the impact of territorial expansion on parasitic zoonoses, using the Pampas gray fox in Argentina as a case study. It highlights how habitat fragmentation and urbanization lead to increased human-animal interactions, which can result in the transmission of zoonotic diseases. The research emphasizes the importance of a One Health approach in addressing these ecological and public health challenges. While the study references prior findings on canid behavior and parasitic infections, it lacks direct empirical data on rabies virus or its specific effects. The implications of the study suggest that education and awareness are crucial for preventing zoonotic disease transmission and promoting ecological balance. However, the general nature of the evidence and reliance on indirect references limit the confidence in the findings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在了解领土扩张对人畜共患病寄生性疾病的影响,特别关注阿根廷的潘帕斯灰狐及其对人类和动物健康的影响。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究考察了城市扩张和栖息地破碎化对阿根廷潘帕斯灰狐种群的影响,分析了该物种与人类群落之间的相互作用。
elements_zh.methods: 该研究参考了之前关于犬科动物响应人类活动而发生的行为和生态变化的研究,并包括关于潘帕斯灰狐中存在寄生人畜共患病的研究数据。
elements_zh.main_results: 在COVID-19大流行期间,灰狐改变了它们的日常活动,潘帕斯灰狐被发现感染宿主各种蠕虫和原生动物,包括犬新孢子虫,它会导致牲畜流产和繁殖失败。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 研究结果强调了与领土扩张和人与动物相互作用相关的生态和健康风险,强调需要采取“同一个健康”方法来解决这些问题。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 该研究强调了了解潘帕斯灰狐的生态作用及其传播人畜共患疾病的潜力、为公共卫生战略和教育举措提供信息的重要性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基于一般观察和对先前研究的参考,这可能会限制对特定因果关系或直接发现的信心。

Given this situation, education plays a crucial role in prevention.The Pampas gray fox is of great ecological importance. Its role as a predator, scavenger, frugivore, and seed disperser has contributed to the development of diverse biomes (Vidal et al., 2025). This animal is a clear example of the importance of One Health education, based on the One Health approach. From an educational perspective, the Science, Technology, and Society (STS) approach is a valuable tool for fostering critical thinking in students, contextualizing learning, and enabling the community to understand different perspectives on an animal. Lampert (2025) has written a book titled "When the Jungle Sits Down to Eat," which analyzes how the welfare of coatis (Nasua nasua), the prevalence of zoonoses, and their behavior are affected by human interaction in Iguazu National Park (Misiones Province, Argentina). Previous research has demonstrated that classroom-based approaches to animal ecology, behavior, welfare, and health risks foster the development of critical thinking skills to prevent contact (Lampert, 2025). While this research focused on the coati, it is essential to address this educational topic with each species that arrives in urban areas, focusing on prevention. Furthermore, various interviews and studies have shown that people become more aware of the potential negative effects of interaction on the animal, rather than on themselves. Therefore, One Health education for prevention must focus not only on people, but also on the risk to species.For the Pampas gray fox, the issue of domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) is a factor within the broader context of habitat alteration. It is important to note that foxes are evolutionarily similar to domestic dogs, not only in terms of anatomy and physiology but also behavior (Fuchs et al., 2009). Peri-urban areas can serve as potential hotspots for pathogen exposure among dog and fox populations; consequently, both domestic dogs and wild foxes may be exposed to the same diseases. The presence of dogs in livestock and rural areas, combined with the encroachment of foxes into these zones (driven by habitat fragmentation and poor waste management) turns these interactions into a transmission pathway for pathogens of veterinary and public health significance (Fuchs et al., 2009).Recent research cites a case in Brazil where domestic dogs may act as bridge hosts for Rickettsia parkeri, transporting infected tick vectors from areas shared with wild foxes (the natural hosts) to vulnerable human populations (Hernández et al., 2021). The same authors who cited the case in Brazil conducted a survey in Chile, finding a higher number of dog-fox interactions (60 interactions) at a coastal peri-urban site compared to two other, less disturbed sites (12 interactions) (Hernández et al., 2021). Societal culture, animal husbandry practices, dietary habits, education levels, conditions of poverty and social marginalization, the availability of potable water, and the rural or urban nature of the habitat are variables that influence the epidemiological complex of various zoonoses (Samartino & Eddi, 2010). Populations in rural and peri-urban areas are in close contact with animals (often involving intensive rearing practices) resulting in significantly higher exposure. Furthermore, the Pampas gray fox frequently ventures into these areas due to their proximity to its natural habitat. Consequently, the level of risk differs between urban and rural zones, although the recent expansion of gated communities has narrowed this gap. It is also worth noting that many canids in rural areas often feed on animal offal; this practice can increase the risk of pathogen transmission to other species-such as the Pampas gray fox-and even directly to humans. Similarly, in urban and periurban spaces, population overcrowding in both zones increases the likelihood of disease transmission and epidemic outbreaks in many regions (Samartino & Eddi, 2010). In the context of territorial expansion, the creation of new neighborhoods in peri-urban areas has facilitated the transmission of various zoonotic diseases to the human population (Samartino & Eddi, 2010).The presence of protozoa (T. caninum), bacteria (Leptospira spp., Brucella spp., antimicrobial-resistant Enterococcus spp.), and viruses (rabies) illustrates how the Pampas gray fox facilitates pathogen transmission (Vidal et al., 2025). Therefore, the Pampas fox should be viewed less as a simple reservoir and more as an indicator of ecological dysfunction, given that health risks are typically associated with transmission via uncontrolled domestic animals rather than the species itself (Vidal et al., 2025). Therefore, the aim is to improve understanding of the spatiotemporal patterns of interspecific contact between invasive and native carnivores, in order to prevent the spread of various pathogens (Hernández et al., 2021). Consequently, education is a fundamental aspect of preventing such transmission. It is worth noting that this education must be contextualized within the specific settings where pathogen transmission is likely to occur. Hence the importance of raising awareness about zoonoses in the various spaces shared by humans and animals, as well as among different animal species. The interaction between animals, humans, and their habitats should be a central focus of modern scientific education; the goal is not merely to learn the definitions and characteristics of various zoonoses, but to understand the environments in which transmission takes place. This enables the public to become informed-for instance, on how to act when encountering animals.In the case of the Pampas Gray Fox, human intervention is impacting its ecology through the use of poison, hunting, roads, and urbanization. This leads us to consider this animal as a model for understanding the capacity to govern shared life with integrity, maintaining ecological and health functions in balance (Vidal et al., 2025). Therefore, education must promote conservation by raising awareness of the human-caused problems affecting this animal and their potential solutions, such as banning poisons, reducing roadkill, managing domestic animals, and promoting coexistence under a genuine "One Health, One Wellbeing" approach, as described by Vidal et al. (2025), in order to achieve the integration of human, animal, and environmental health in urban planning.The STS approach to one health prevention education should incorporate the following elements, drawing on the book of Lampert (2019): Mainstream the "One Health, One Wellbeing" or Conservation Medicine approach. In the case of the Pampas gray fox, education regarding the animal should not be conducted in isolation-treating the animal's physiology and habitat, zoonoses, and territorial/urban expansion as separate topics. Instead, the issue must be addressed through an integrated, cross-cutting approach that acknowledges its complexity.  Contextualize instruction across different settings. Studying and understanding human-animal contact differs depending on whether the setting is rural, peri-urban, or urban. Local wildlife must be identified, along with the ways in which the transmission of microorganisms between species could be altered.  Teach about animal feeding practices. It is essential to understand the risks posed to the ecosystem by feeding domestic canids animal offal or raw meat that has not undergone sanitary or food safety inspection.  Develop educational initiatives grounded in health education, environmental education, and food education. In the case of Argentina, it is worth noting that environmental education and food education are mandated by law.

papers.title: Supporting rabies elimination with evidence: Quantifying domestic dog populations, ecology and vaccination economics
papers.abstract: Rabies remains a major public health threat in many low and middle-income countries, with domestic dogs as the principal reservoir. Effective control requires sound planning, implementation, and monitoring, based on reliable data on dog populations, their movements, and vaccination costs. This thesis had three objectives: to estimate the size of the domestic dog population in Machakos County, Kenya, to characterise movement ecology across areas with different human population densities, and to evaluate the implementation and costs of mass dog vaccination to inform county-level planning and long-term sustainability. I used household surveys, photographic sight–resight methods, GPS tracking, and economic modelling. The cross-sectional household survey estimated an owned dog population of 421,079, nearly double prior national projections, implying greater resource needs for control and a stronger case for education on responsible ownership. In a rapidly urbanising area, the free-roaming dog population was estimated at 3,807 dogs (95% CI: 1,780–5,833) when extrapolated to the total administrative area, and 3,150 dogs (95% CI: 1,473–4,826) when extrapolated to the inhabited area, with a density of 108 dogs per km2 and a human-to-dog ratio ranging from approximately 1:24 to 1:30. Household data indicated that most free-roaming dogs were owned, highlighting the importance of improved confinement and responsible ownership. To assess spatial behaviour, 100 free-roaming dogs were GPS-tracked in low-density and high-density settings. Dogs in low-density areas had larger home ranges, while those in high-density areas exhibited more spatially constrained movement but slightly higher movement intensity. Movement patterns were primarily influenced by population density and age. These differences suggest that in rural settings, vaccination campaigns must cover larger geographic areas to reach widely roaming dogs, while in high-density settings, effective coverage can be achieved within smaller, more localised areas. The cost evaluation drew on a four-year county campaign that vaccinated 136,143 dogs. The mean cost per dog vaccinated was USD 2.41. Coordination, vaccines, and personnel were the main cost drivers. A Monte Carlo simulation estimated that achieving 70% vaccination coverage across the county would require a median annual cost of KES 47.2 million (approximately USD 0.36 million), exceeding the current Machakos County veterinary budget of KES 35.5 million. Across alternative operational scenarios, total campaign costs remained broadly similar (approximately KES 55 million), indicating that changes in campaign design had a limited impact on overall expenditure. However, substantial differences were observed in workforce requirements. A 360-day delivery schedule reduced the number of teams required by approximately 75% compared with a 60-day intensive campaign, offering a more feasible approach where workforce capacity is constrained. Vaccine donation reduced total programme costs by 24.5%, representing a substantial reduction in overall expenditure, with delivery-related components, particularly personnel and transport, continuing to account for a large share of total costs. Overall, the thesis demonstrates the value of integrating demographic, ecological, and financial evidence to plan rabies control efforts. I provide locally grounded estimates of owned dog population, movement patterns that guide spatial targeting, and realistic costs for campaign planning. These insights support scalable, context-responsive strategies for Machakos County and similar endemic settings.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 这项横断面家庭调查估计了肯尼亚马查科斯县养狗的数量,并描述了不同人口密度地区的运动生态特征。该研究还评估了大众狗 疫苗接种 的实施和成本,为县级规划和长期可持续性提供信息。
elements_zh.methods: 我使用家庭调查、摄影复视方法、GPS 跟踪和经济模型来估计狗的数量、描述运动模式并评估 疫苗接种 成本。
elements_zh.main_results: 横断面家庭调查估计,养狗数量为 421,079 只,几乎是之前全国预测的两倍。流动模式主要受人口密度和年龄的影响。与 60 天的密集活动相比,360 天的交付计划将所需团队数量减少了约 75%。

papers.title_zh: 用证据支持消除 狂犬病:量化家犬数量、生态和 疫苗接种 经济学
papers.source_body_en: Rabies remains a major public health threat in many low and middle-income countries, with domestic dogs as the principal reservoir. Effective control requires sound planning, implementation, and monitoring, based on reliable data on dog populations, their movements, and vaccination costs. This thesis had three objectives: to estimate the size of the domestic dog population in Machakos County, Kenya, to characterise movement ecology across areas with different human population densities, and to evaluate the implementation and costs of mass dog vaccination to inform county-level planning and long-term sustainability. I used household surveys, photographic sight–resight methods, GPS tracking, and economic modelling. The cross-sectional household survey estimated an owned dog population of 421,079, nearly double prior national projections, implying greater resource needs for control and a stronger case for education on responsible ownership. In a rapidly urbanising area, the free-roaming dog population was estimated at 3,807 dogs (95% CI: 1,780–5,833) when extrapolated to the total administrative area, and 3,150 dogs (95% CI: 1,473–4,826) when extrapolated to the inhabited area, with a density of 108 dogs per km2 and a human-to-dog ratio ranging from approximately 1:24 to 1:30. Household data indicated that most free-roaming dogs were owned, highlighting the importance of improved confinement and responsible ownership. To assess spatial behaviour, 100 free-roaming dogs were GPS-tracked in low-density and high-density settings. Dogs in low-density areas had larger home ranges, while those in high-density areas exhibited more spatially constrained movement but slightly higher movement intensity. Movement patterns were primarily influenced by population density and age. These differences suggest that in rural settings, vaccination campaigns must cover larger geographic areas to reach widely roaming dogs, while in high-density settings, effective coverage can be achieved within smaller, more localised areas. The cost evaluation drew on a four-year county campaign that vaccinated 136,143 dogs. The mean cost per dog vaccinated was USD 2.41. Coordination, vaccines, and personnel were the main cost drivers. A Monte Carlo simulation estimated that achieving 70% vaccination coverage across the county would require a median annual cost of KES 47.2 million (approximately USD 0.36 million), exceeding the current Machakos County veterinary budget of KES 35.5 million. Across alternative operational scenarios, total campaign costs remained broadly similar (approximately KES 55 million), indicating that changes in campaign design had a limited impact on overall expenditure. However, substantial differences were observed in workforce requirements. A 360-day delivery schedule reduced the number of teams required by approximately 75% compared with a 60-day intensive campaign, offering a more feasible approach where workforce capacity is constrained. Vaccine donation reduced total programme costs by 24.5%, representing a substantial reduction in overall expenditure, with delivery-related components, particularly personnel and transport, continuing to account for a large share of total costs. Overall, the thesis demonstrates the value of integrating demographic, ecological, and financial evidence to plan rabies control efforts. I provide locally grounded estimates of owned dog population, movement patterns that guide spatial targeting, and realistic costs for campaign planning. These insights support scalable, context-responsive strategies for Machakos County and similar endemic settings.

analysis_zh.methods: 我使用家庭调查、摄影复视方法、GPS 跟踪和经济模型来估计狗的数量、描述运动模式并评估 疫苗接种 成本。
analysis_zh.main_results: 横断面家庭调查估计,养狗数量为 421,079 只,几乎是之前全国预测的两倍。流动模式主要受人口密度和年龄的影响。与 60 天的密集活动相比,360 天的交付计划将所需团队数量减少了约 75%。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 这些差异表明,在农村环境中,疫苗接种 活动必须覆盖更大的地理区域才能覆盖广泛漫游的狗,而在高密度环境中,可以在更小、更局部的区域内实现有效覆盖。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果通过提供基于当地的养狗数量估计、指导空间目标的运动模式以及活动规划的实际成本,支持马查科斯县和类似流行环境的可扩展、因地制宜的战略。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究基于横断面调查和外推,这可能会限制结果的普遍性。证据只是抽象的,研究结果的可信度中等。

papers.title: Viral metagenomics of synanthropic urban bats: A surveillance strategy for uncovering potentially zoonotic viruses
papers.abstract: Abstract Bats are natural reservoirs for diverse viruses, including coronaviruses, filoviruses, and paramyxoviruses, many leading to zoonotic spillover events and demanding an integrated surveillance. Here, we present a framework that leverages Brazil’s rabies passive surveillance program to detect bat-borne viruses. Using an algorithm to select representative specimens from 2,422 bats collected across São Paulo state, we submitted 150 paired lung and intestine samples to nanopore metagenomic sequencing. We detected 98 viral contigs from 12 families of public health relevance, including Arenaviridae, Coronaviridae , and Paramyxoviridae . Notably, the approach identified a previously unknown filovirus in bats in the Americas, validating the framework’s capacity for epidemic preparedness. These findings reveal an undetected viral diversity and demonstrate how existing animal surveillance can monitor pathogen threats. Crucially, in a workshop involving multisectoral One Health experts in Brazil, this framework was validated as a scalable model for national expansion, adapted for low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). One-sentence summary line The study introduces a viral surveillance method using metagenomics in bats, offering a scalable, cost-effective model for operationalizing One Health surveillance, especially relevant to low- and middle-income countries.

papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 蝙蝠对多种病毒具有天然的 储存宿主,包括冠状病毒、丝状病毒和副粘病毒,许多病毒会导致人畜共患 跨物种溢出 事件并需要整合的 监测。在这里,我们提出了一个利用巴西的 狂犬病 被动 监测 程序来检测蝙蝠传播的病毒的框架。我们使用一种算法从圣保罗州收集的 2,422 只蝙蝠中选择代表性样本,并将 150 个配对的肺和肠道样本提交给纳米孔宏基因组测序。我们检测到来自 12 个与公共卫生相关的科的 98 个病毒重叠群,包括沙粒病毒科、冠状病毒科和副粘病毒科。值得注意的是,该方法在美洲蝙蝠中发现了一种以前未知的丝状病毒,验证了该框架的流行病防范能力。这些发现揭示了未被检测到的病毒多样性,并证明了现有动物 监测 如何监测病原体威胁。至关重要的是,在巴西举行的由多部门 One Health 专家参加的研讨会上,该框架被验证为国家扩张的可扩展模型,适合低收入和中等收入国家 (LMIC)。该研究介绍了一种利用蝙蝠宏基因组学的病毒 监测 方法,为实施 One Health 监测 提供了一种可扩展、具有成本效益的模型,特别是与低收入和中等收入国家相关。

papers.title: Microplastics in Big Brown Bats: Associations with county level Urbanization
papers.abstract: As plastics degrade, they form microplastics (MPs) that can be ingested or inhaled and subsequently accumulate in animal tissues. Eptesicus fuscus (big brown bats) are widespread North American insectivores that can serve as bioindicators of MP exposure through airborne, aquatic, and insect-mediated pathways. In this study, we evaluated 18 bats across six counties in North Carolina, USA. We assessed MP presence in the heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract and tested whether urbanization predicts MP burden. An urbanization index was developed using population density, impervious surface cover, and tree canopy metrics. Specimens were obtained opportunistically as a byproduct of the rabies testing.

News Montgomery County Health and Animal Services Officials Remind Residents to Avoid Contact with Wildlife Following Confirmed Rabies Case in Beaver News Release Montgomery County Health and Animal Services Officials Remind Residents to Avoid Contact with Wildlife Following Confirmed Rabies Case in Beaver August 21, 2026 Animal Services Media Contact Nordea Lewis Public Information Officer Nordea.Lewis@montgomerycountymd.gov 240-777-6527 Montgomery County health and animal services officials are reminding residents to avoid contact with wildlife following confirmation that a beaver found dead near Seneca Creek State Park tested positive for rabies. Rabies is a viral disease that affects mammals and is primarily transmitted through the bite of an infected animal. The disease is nearly always fatal once symptoms begin, but prompt medical evaluation and preventive treatment following a potential exposure are highly effective. On Thursday, Aug. 13, a 10-year-old girl attending a summer camp was attacked and bitten by a beaver while in Seneca Creek State Park near Berryville Road. The child was taken to a local hospital for treatment. On Monday, Aug. 17, Maryland Department of Natural Resources (DNR) staff located a deceased beaver in the area. Testing by the Maryland Department of Health confirmed on Wednesday, Aug. 19, that the animal was positive for rabies. DNR and health officials have not been able to determine whether the rabid beaver is the same animal involved in the Aug. 13 attack. “Wildlife should always be observed from a safe distance,” said Caroline Hairfield, executive director of the Office of Animal Services. “This confirmed rabies case is an important reminder not to touch, feed or attempt to help wild animals, even if they appear sick, injured or unusually calm. Keep pets away from wildlife, use a leash when walking dogs and ensure your pets’ rabies vaccinations are current. If you have contact with a wild animal, seek medical guidance promptly and report the incident so the appropriate agencies can respond.” DNR continues to search the area for additional sick beavers or other wildlife. A portion of Seneca Creek State Park near the location of the incident, including approximately one mile of trail and river access points, remains closed. Other areas of the park remain open. According to DNR, there is currently no indication of a rabies outbreak in the County. “Finding rabies in a beaver is rare, but it serves as a stark reminder that the virus can affect any mammal,” said Dr. Kisha Davis, Montgomery County health officer. “We urge residents to keep a safe distance from all wildlife, ensure pets are vaccinated and report any bites or unusual animal behavior immediately.” Residents Urged to Avoid Contact with Wildlife Residents should not approach, touch, feed, capture, or otherwise interact with wildlife, including animals that appear friendly, sick, injured, disoriented, or dead. A change in an animal’s normal behavior can be a warning sign, but the absence of unusual behavior does not mean an animal is safe to handle. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises people to leave wildlife alone and not to touch injured wildlife. Residents should also keep pets away from wildlife and ensure dogs, cats, and ferrets are current on their rabies vaccinations. In Maryland, rabies is most frequently found in wildlife, including raccoons, foxes, skunks, and bats. Domestic animals may also be at risk. What to Do After a Possible Exposure Anyone who is bitten, scratched, or may have otherwise been exposed to wildlife or an unfamiliar animal should: Immediately wash the wound or exposed area thoroughly with soap and water. Promptly seek medical care and public-health guidance. Report potential animal exposures in Montgomery County by calling the police non-emergency line at 301-279-8000. Call 911 if an animal attack is in progress or there is an immediate threat to life or safety. Residents should never attempt to capture or handle a wild animal themselves, even if the animal appears injured, sick, or dead. For additional information about rabies, animal bites and what to do following a potential exposure, visit the Montgomery County Office of Animal Services' Bites and Rabies webpage. For information about the Seneca Creek State Park incident and current park closures, visit the Maryland Department of Natural Resources update. # # # Media Contact: Nordea Lewis, Nordea.lewis@montgomerycountymd.gov or 240-962-0315 Nordea Lewis Public Information Officer Nordea.Lewis@montgomerycountymd.gov 240-777-6527 Animal Services Follow the Public Information Office - en Español Follow Montgomery County Government Sign up for the Press Releases

news.content: A Commonwealth of Virginia WebsiteAn official website of the Commonwealth of Virginia Here's how you knowAn official websiteHere's how you know To ensure accurate screen reader translation, please ensure you have the proper language packs installed.English ▼ ኣማርኛ العربية الفصحى 简化字 正體字 Français हिंदी 한국어 Español Tagalog اردو Tiếng Việt Find a Commonwealth Resource Skip to content Roanoke Health District Search for: × About How Do I A-Z Index Locations Data Clinicians Newsroom Contact Virginia Department of Health > Roanoke Health District > Rabies Alerts > Rabies Case Alert – Roanoke City – Melrose Avenue NW , Roanoke Rabies Case Alert – Roanoke City – Melrose Avenue NW , Roanoke Posted on August 18, 2026August 18, 2026 by shannonbowles Rabies Case Alert - August 17th, 2026 For more information contact: Roanoke City and Alleghany Health Districts (RCAHD) Environmental Health Division • (540) 204-9764 Rabies Case Alert August 17th, 2026 For more information contact: Roanoke City and Alleghany Health Districts (RCAHD) Environmental Health Division (540) 204-9764 RABIES CASE CONFIRMED IN ROANOKE CITY, VA Health officials have confirmed the presence of rabies in the area of: Melrose Avenue NW and Viewmont Street NW Roanoke, VA 24017 A raccoon was confirmed positive for rabies by the Virginia Department of Health. It was collected on 08/11/2026 near Melrose Avenue NW and Viewmont Street NW in Roanoke City. Please contact the RCAHD Environmental Health Division or Roanoke City Animal Control if you know of any possible human or animal contact with this animal. Rabies is a deadly disease caused by a virus that attacks the nervous system. It is preventable in domestic animals through vaccinations, but is fatal to both animals and humans if left untreated. Exposure to rabies is considered: any time a bite or scratch (or other circumstance) allows saliva or central nervous system tissue from a potentially rabid animal to enter an open, fresh wound. when rabid tissue enters a mucous membrane via the eye, mouth, or nose. The Code of Virginia §3.2-6521 requires pet owners to maintain current rabies vaccinations for dogs and cats aged four months and older. Citizens should not approach or touch any wild or stray animals and should report any abnormal animal behavior to their local animal control dispatcher. All animal bites and rabies exposures (from wild and domestic animals) must be reported to the RCAHD Environmental Health Division at 540-204-9764. To help prevent the spread of rabies, everyone should: AVOID contact with wild animals and domestic animals you do not know. REPORT injured or threatening animals. VACCINATE all of your dogs, cats and ferrets, and keep their vaccinations current. WASH the wound with soap and water. Don’t panic. Call your doctor and the local health department if you are exposed to an animal with rabies. Call your veterinarian and local animal control if your pet is exposed to an animal with rabies. DayakDaily MAIN LOCAL BEYOND SARAWAK SPORTS LEISURE KENYALANG PORTRAITS IBAN SECTION VIDEOS ADS Sarawak human rabies fatality rate hits 93 pct, with 87 deaths out of 94 cases since 2017 Aug 22, 2026 @ 14:51 Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Linkedin Email Print Telegram Wee (seated, centre) along with other distinguished guests and participants at the Stop Rabies Carnival 2026 launching ceremony on Aug 22, 2026. Photo: TVS Advertisement By DayakDaily Team KOTA SAMARAHAN, Aug 22: Rabies has claimed 87 human lives in Sarawak since July 2017, pushing the fatality rate among the 94 human cases recorded during the period to nearly 93 per cent. According to a report by TVS, Sarawak Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian said the alarming figure underscored the need for immediate action following any animal bite or scratch. Advertisement “Vaccinate your pets every year. Responsible pet ownership can create active protection within the local community. “If bitten or scratched, clean the wound and seek treatment immediately. Wash any animal bite or scratch immediately with soap under running water for at least 15 minutes, then proceed directly to the nearest health clinic,” he said in his speech read by Kuching South City Council (MBKS) Dato Wee Hong Seng at the launching ceremony of the Stop Rabies Carnival 2026 here today. He stressed that immediate treatment is crucial, as waiting for rabies symptoms to appear could be fatal once clinical symptoms begin. Meanwhile, data from the Sarawak Veterinary Services Department verified as of Aug 20 showed that 23 dogs and three cats had tested positive for rabies so far this year, said Dr Sim. He said the fight against rabies required a collective effort involving all segments of society, including children and youths, pet owners, non-governmental organisations, academic researchers, healthcare workers and community leaders. “Rabies prevention across all sectors of society will help Sarawak achieve its State target while contributing to the global mission of Zero Human Rabies Deaths by 2030,” he said. — DayakDaily Advertisement RELATED ARTICLESMORE FROM AUTHOR Dalat must move beyond raw materials to unlock greater economic value, says Premier Sarawak plans stronger health data protection amid growing AI, digital tech use Deputy Premier: AI can bridge Sarawak’s healthcare gaps, but human compassion comes first Ads Get news FASTER! analysis.brief_en: Rabies has been a significant public health concern in Sarawak, Malaysia, with 87 human deaths recorded since July 2017, resulting in a fatality rate of 93% among 94 reported cases. The Sarawak Veterinary Services Department confirmed 23 dogs and three cats tested positive for rabies this year, as of August 20, 2026. Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian highlighted the urgency of immediate action following any animal bite or scratch, urging prompt wound cleaning and treatment. He emphasized the need for responsible pet ownership and collective efforts across all sectors of society to combat rabies. The Stop Rabies Carnival 2026 was launched to raise awareness and promote prevention measures, aiming to achieve the state's rabies control targets and contribute to the global mission of Zero Human Rabies Deaths by 2030. The response includes public health campaigns and community engagement, with a focus on education and early intervention.

LET’S READ SUARA SARAWAK/ NEW SARAWAK TRIBUNE E-PAPER FOR FREE AS ​​EARLY AS 2 AM EVERY DAY. CLICK LINK KOTA SAMARAHAN: Sarawak has recorded 94 human rabies cases with 87 deaths since July 2017. Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian said the fatality rate stood at nearly 93 per cent, based on data verified with the Sarawak Health Department (JKNS) on Aug 20. He said 23 dogs and three cats had been confirmed positive for rabies so far this year, according to data from the Department of Veterinary Services Sarawak (DVSS) verified on the same date. “Every bite, nip, or scratch from any animal must be treated as an immediate health emergency,” he said. He urged the public to vaccinate pets annually and to wash any bite or scratch under running water with soap for at least 15 minutes before seeking treatment at the nearest health clinic. Wee delivers speech on behalf of Dr Sim. He said this in a speech read out by Kuching South City Council mayor, Datuk Wee Hong Seng during the launch of the Stop Rabies 2026: Rabies Education Carnival here today (Aug 22). The carnival, jointly organised with the Malaysia One Health University Network (MyOHUN) and funded by Boehringer Ingelheim, also honoured the top six finalist school teams in the ‘Rabies Hero Ambassador’ competition, representing seven districts across Sarawak. Dr Sim thanked Boehringer Ingelheim for bringing its global ‘Stop Rabies’ programme to the state, and MyOHUN, along with lecturers and student volunteers from UNIMAS, Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) and Universiti Malaysia Kelantan (UMK), for supporting school outreach efforts. It added that the initiative aligns with the state’s Post COVID-19 Development Strategy (PCDS 2030) and the global goal of achieving zero human rabies deaths by 2030. Also present were UNIMAS Vice Chancellor Professor Dr Ahmad Hata Rasit, MyOHUN President Professor Dr Abdul Rahman Omar, and Boehringer Ingelheim’s Head of Business Segment for Companion Animals, Dr Evonne Lim. Wee (third left), Ahmad Hata (fourth left) and other dignitaries pose for a group photo with winners of ‘Rabies Hero Ambassador’ competition for high school category. The event, organized with the Malaysia One Health University Network (MyOHUN) and funded by Boehringer Ingelheim, also celebrated the top six finalist school teams in the ‘Rabies Hero Ambassador’ competition, representing seven districts. Dr Sim emphasized the importance of annual pet vaccinations and immediate treatment for animal bites, urging the public to take preventive measures. The initiative aligns with Sarawak’s Post COVID-19 Development Strategy (PCDS 2030) and the global goal of zero human rabies deaths by 2030.

GRAND TRAVERSE COUNTY — A bat found inside a Grand Traverse County residence tested positive for rabies after possible human exposure, the Grand Traverse County Health Department said. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services conducted the testing, and all identified as exposed are receiving post-exposure medical care. Health officials said rabies spreads through the saliva of infected mammals, typically through a bite or scratch. The disease is almost always fatal once symptoms appear but can be prevented with prompt medical care and vaccination after exposure. Advertisement Bats are Michigan’s most common rabies carrier, officials said, and bites and scratches can be hard to see. As of Aug. 19, 36 bats and one skunk in Michigan have tested positive; any direct contact with a bat should be treated as a potential exposure, officials said. Residents are urged to avoid contact with wild animals, including bats, raccoons, skunks and foxes, and to keep pets vaccinated against rabies, including cats, dogs, ferrets, horses, cattle and sheep. Officials also recommended sealing openings that could allow bats into homes and not handling wildlife with bare hands. If a bat is found in a home, residents should not release it, officials said. They should safely contain the bat without direct handling and call GTCHD at 231-995-6051 to discuss testing and possible exposure, and should not bring a bat to the health department without calling first to set an appointment. Anyone bitten or scratched by an animal, or who has contact with a bat, should seek medical attention immediately. For general questions about bat exposures and rabies post-exposure prophylaxis, contact GTCHD at 231-995-6125 or visit the MDHHS Michigan Emerging Disease – Rabies resource page. news.content_zh: 2026 年 8 月 21 日,在密歇根州大特拉弗斯县的一处住宅中确认了一只 狂犬病 阳性蝙蝠。密歇根州卫生与公众服务部进行了检测,可能与人类接触过的个人正在接受接触后医疗护理。卫生官员强调,狂犬病 通过受感染哺乳动物的唾液传播,通常通过咬伤或抓伤传播。一旦出现症状,这种疾病几乎总是致命的,但及时的医疗护理和 疫苗接种 可以预防它。建议居民避免接触包括蝙蝠在内的野生动物,并为宠物接种疫苗。他们还应安全地控制在家中发现的任何蝙蝠,并联系大特拉弗斯县卫生部门寻求进一步指导。卫生部门提供了如何处理蝙蝠暴露的具体说明,并建议密封开口以防止蝙蝠进入房屋。

Summary In Sarawak, 26 animals, including 23 dogs and three cats, have tested positive for rabies in 2026, according to the Department of Veterinary Services Sarawak. Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian emphasized the severe risk and high fatality rate of rabies, which is nearly universally fatal once symptoms appear but entirely preventable through vaccination and responsible pet ownership. At the Stop Rabies 2026: Rabies Education Carnival, Dr Sim urged the public to treat any animal bites as health emergencies and stressed the importance of collective efforts to eliminate human rabies deaths by 2030. The event, supported by multiple organizations, also celebrated winners of the Rabies Hero Ambassador 2026 competition. First Published: Saturday, 22 Aug 2026 4:23 PM MYT × Subscribe to Newsletter Subscribe KOTA SAMARAHAN, Aug 22 — Three cats were among 26 animals confirmed positive for rabies in Sarawak so far this year, with the remaining 23 cases involving dogs. Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian said the figures, based on data from the Department of Veterinary Services Sarawak (DVSS), were verified as of Aug 20. “As a medical doctor and your Minister for Public Health, I must remind everyone of the sobering reality. Since July 2017, Sarawak has recorded 94 human rabies cases with 87 deaths, data verified with JKNS on Aug 20, 2026. That is a fatality rate near 93 per cent. Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is almost universally fatal. Yet, it is 100 per cent preventable. “From the animal health side, for 2026, to date, a total of 23 dogs and three cats were confirmed as positive rabies cases, data from DVSS, verified on Aug 20, 2026,” he said in his speech read by Kuching South City Council (MBKS) Mayor Datuk Wee Hong Seng at the launch of the Stop Rabies 2026: Rabies Education Carnival at Universiti Malaysia Sarawak (Unimas), here on Saturday. Dr Sim, who is also minister for public health, housing and local government, reminded the public that every bite, nip or scratch from an animal must be treated as an immediate health emergency. “Ensure your community knows two simple rules: vaccinate your pets annually, and practise responsible pet ownership. Regular vaccination creates an important protective buffer for the entire neighbourhood. “Wash and run: immediately wash any animal bite or scratch under running water with soap for at least 15 minutes, then go straight to the nearest health clinic. Do not wait for symptoms to appear,” he said. Dr Sim said achieving the target of eliminating human rabies in Sarawak required every citizen to play an active role. “By taking ownership of rabies prevention across all sectors of society, we will fulfil our state target and contribute to the global mission of Zero Human Rabies Deaths by 2030,” he added. The Stop Rabies 2026: Rabies Education Carnival was organised with the Malaysia One Health University Network (MyOHUN), with support from Boehringer Ingelheim Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and involved agencies including the Sarawak Health Department (JKNS), DVSS and the Sarawak Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SSPCA). The event also saw the presentation of certificates and awards for the Rabies Hero Ambassador 2026 competition. In the secondary school category, SMK Jalan Arang emerged as champion, followed by SMK Tinggi Kuching in second place and SMK Sri Aman in third. In the primary school category, SJK(C) Chung Hua Sematan emerged as champion, followed by SJK(C) Chung Hua Bintulu 2 in second place and SJK(C) Sebiew Chinese Bintulu in third. Also present at the event were Unimas Vice Chancellor Prof Dr Ahmad Hata Rasit, MyOHUN president Prof Dr Abdul Rahman Omar, Boehringer Ingelheim Malaysia, Singapore & Indonesia head of business segment companion animals Dr Evonne Lim, and SSPCA president Datin Sri Dona Drury Wee. — The Borneo Post You May Also Like Related Articles Malaysia / 7 h ago Police: Seven men arrested after viral car park fight in front of Bintulu grocery store Malaysia / 7 h ago Elderly man, neighbour trapped on 14th‐floor ledge rescued unharmed by Penang firefighters Malaysia / 7 h ago NSC blocks Datasonic takeover, vows to shield MyKad and passport identity under strict oversight Just IN 7 h ago Police: Seven men arrested after viral car park fight in front of Bintulu grocery store 7 h ago Elderly man, neighbour trapped on 14th‐floor ledge rescued unharmed by Penang firefighters 7 h ago NSC blocks Datasonic takeover, vows to shield MyKad and passport identity under strict oversight

news.source_body_en: Sarawak has confirmed 26 rabies cases in 2026, including three cats and 23 dogs, according to the Department of Veterinary Services Sarawak. Deputy Premier Datuk Amar Dr Sim Kui Hian highlighted the severe risk and high fatality rate of rabies, which is nearly universally fatal once symptoms appear but entirely preventable through vaccination and responsible pet ownership. Since July 2017, the state has recorded 94 human rabies cases with 87 deaths, resulting in a fatality rate of approximately 93 per cent. The data was verified as of August 20, 2026. The Stop Rabies 2026: Rabies Education Carnival was organized with support from multiple organizations, including the Malaysia One Health University Network (MyOHUN), Boehringer Ingelheim Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia, and involved agencies such as the Sarawak Health Department (JKNS), DVSS, and the Sarawak Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SSPCA). The event also celebrated winners of the Rabies Hero Ambassador 2026 competition, emphasizing the need for collective efforts to eliminate human rabies deaths by 2030.
